Circum Simson

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Four dots sit on one circle, and two straight lines run from the opposite dots P and Q. Watch where the lines cross as you move the dots.
How to play: Drag a blue dot with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the crossing lines, the feet, the midpoints and the path of the crossing point; press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Drag P around the circle and the two long lines turn with it, yet they always cross at a right angle, and their crossing point keeps to a smaller circle. The original cut-the-knot article, now illustrated with a GeoGebra figure, describes exactly the Java applet ported here.

Two lines, one right angle

Drop perpendiculars from P onto the three sides. Their feet lie on one straight line, the Simson line. The point Q is opposite P on the circumcircle, and its three feet give a second Simson line. The two are always perpendicular. The logic test checks 300 random triangles and 72 places for P on the starting circle: the angle is 90° to better than a millionth of a radian.

The path of the crossing point

As P moves, the crossing point M traces a circle whose centre is halfway between the circumcentre O and the orthocenter H, and whose radius is half the circumradius. That is the nine-point circle: it also passes through the three side midpoints A', B', C'. The test confirms that M stays on it, and that A' is the midpoint of PaQa, just as the article's proof says.

Why the lines are at right angles

Hubert Shutrick's proof uses cyclic quadrilaterals: C, P, Pa, Pb lie on one circle and C, Q, Qb, Qa on another. Equal inscribed angles give angle PaPbC = angle QQaQb; since one pair of sides is perpendicular, so is the other: PaPb ⟂ QaQb. Tick "angles" for the circles and "perpendiculars" for the six feet.

A small applet quirk

The applet's own foot routine returns P itself when P lies within sqrt(0.1) of the end of a side. Very near a vertex — or near the point opposite it, where Q sits — that snaps one foot and the exact theorem is off by a hair. The port keeps the applet's rule so the test matches its computation on every drawing; outside that tiny zone the claims hold to a ten-millionth of the circle's radius. The applet shows the traced points only while you drag; this page draws the whole circle for you.

Tick Simson lines and Trace circle, then drag P all the way round: the orange dots draw the nine-point circle. Press Reset to return to the starting triangle.
